e.etymology: A spelling of Donna, a name made in the 19th century from the Italian word donna, lady. Dona is also the Portuguese title of respect for a woman.
A pet form of Jan, Jane or Janet, all feminine forms of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. In Dutch and Afrikaans Jannie is a pet form of Jan.
A spelling of Deirdre, from Old Irish Derdriu, the tragic heroine of Irish legend. The meaning of the name is unknown.
namesakes: Deidre Hall (Marlena on Days of Our Lives)

e.etymology: A coinage joining Lu, as in Lucy or Louise, with Anne.
namesakes: Luanne Platter (Hank's niece on King of the Hill)

e.etymology: A spelling of Dominique with two letters transposed. Dominique is the French form of Dominic, from Latin dominicus, belonging to the Lord.
e.note: Looks like a typo for Dominique, so it will often be corrected.

e.etymology: Generally linked to Greek arete, virtue or excellence. Aretha Franklin made it famous; American use peaked in 1968, the year after Respect.
namesakes: Aretha Franklin (singer known as the Queen of Soul)

assoc.t: Aretha Franklin, the Queen of Soul

e.etymology: A spelling of Jessica, first used by Shakespeare in The Merchant of Venice and probably drawn from Iscah, a Hebrew name in Genesis. The single-s form is common in Spanish.
A spelling of Brian, an Irish name probably built on a Celtic word for high or noble and made famous by the high king Brian Boru. The same spelling shows in the surname O'Brien.
From the surname, also spelled Parnell, which comes from Pernel, a medieval English form of the woman's name Petronilla. Bonanza star Pernell Roberts brought it attention in the early 1960s.
A spelling of Jeremy with two letters transposed. Jeremy is the English form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the Lord exalts.
e.note: Looks like a typo for Jeremy, so it will often be corrected.

e.etymology: A variant of Melvin, which comes from the Scottish surname Melville, itself from Malleville, a place in Normandy.
A spelling of Mabel reshaped to look like May plus Bell. Mabel is short for Amabel, from Latin amabilis, lovable.
In America it looks like a short form of names ending in -zetta, such as Rozetta and Lizetta. In Greek, Zetta is a pet form of Elisavet, or Elizabeth.
In most cases a pet form of Beatrice, and sometimes a nickname built on the initial B. It matches French bébé, baby.
namesakes: Bebe Neuwirth (Lilith on Cheers and Frasier)
e.note: Reads as bebé, the Spanish and French word for baby.

e.etymology: The French feminine of Henri, coined in the 17th century. Henry comes from Germanic words for home and ruler. English has favored the forms Harriet and Henrietta.
A phonetic spelling of Italian Marcello, from Latin Marcellus, a diminutive of Marcus, the Roman name linked to the god Mars.
A spelling of Robin, a medieval pet form of Robert, from Germanic words for fame and bright.
An American spelling of Antoinette, the French feminine pet form of Antoine, or Anthony, which goes back to the Roman family name Antonius.
From a surname, used as a first name mainly in the American South. It reads as Ray plus the place-name ending -ford.
The French spelling of a name that came through Greek Rhoxane from an Old Persian word for bright or shining. Roxane was the wife of Alexander the Great and is the heroine of Cyrano de Bergerac.
An elaboration of Laura or Lauren, both from Latin laurus, laurel, by way of Laurentius. French has the matching form Laurène.
A phonetic spelling of Portia, from Latin Porcia, the feminine of the Roman family name Porcius, built on porcus, pig. Shakespeare's heroine in The Merchant of Venice made Portia familiar.
namesakes: Porsha Williams (The Real Housewives of Atlanta cast member)
e.note: Sounds the same as Porsche, the sports car, which is what many people will hear first.

assoc.t: Porsche, the German sports car maker (same sound)
Porsha Williams of The Real Housewives of Atlanta

e.etymology: A 1990s spelling that sits between Ciara, the Irish name from ciar, dark-haired, and Sierra, Spanish for mountain range. Most bearers say it like Sierra.
Name references group it with Lona, a short form of Leona, the feminine of Leo, lion. It also reads as a feminine form of Lonnie.
A spelling of Christopher with the h dropped. Christopher comes from Greek Christophoros, joining Christos with pherein, to bear.
e.note: Looks like a typo for Christopher, so it will often be corrected.

e.etymology: A spelling of Monty, the pet form of Montgomery and Montague, both Norman French place-name surnames that begin with mont, hill.
The Italian form of Hilda, which began as a short form of Germanic names containing hild, battle.
A spelling of Wendy, the name J. M. Barrie made famous with Wendy Darling in Peter Pan in 1904.
namesakes: Wendi McLendon-Covey (actress in The Goldbergs and Bridesmaids)
